title: Lesson 3: Giving, advocacy, and being a multiplier
html:
Your giving

Even modest donations to effective charities can do a great deal of good. If you’re earning an average income in the Netherlands, you’re in the richest few percent of people globally. This isn’t meant to induce guilt. It’s a factual observation about the opportunity you have: because of the vast inequality in global income, your money goes much further when directed to the most cost-effective interventions in the global south than when spent on additional consumption. If you want to see where you sit globally, try the How Rich Am I calculator. Most people on a Dutch salary are startled.

The argument behind this comes from the philosopher Peter Singer. If you can prevent something very bad from happening at little cost to yourself, you should. An average Dutch income makes that cost small. Week 2 showed how far a well-directed euro can travel; Singer’s argument is about why that matters.

Read: Peter Singer, The Life You Can Save, chapters 1–2 (free download) (~30 mins).

The core insight is about marginal impact. The hundredth euro you spend on yourself each month buys you very little extra wellbeing compared with the ninety-ninth. The same euro, given to a highly effective charity, can buy far more wellbeing for someone living in extreme poverty. This is diminishing marginal returns applied to global inequality.

Two organisations can help you give effectively:

  • Doneer Effectief: a Dutch organisation that helps you find and donate to highly effective charities, with recommendations across cause areas and Dutch-language support. If you’re comfortable with Dutch and just want a simple way to give, we recommend using their platform.

  • Giving What We Can: an international community of people committed to effective giving, with charity recommendations and a public pledge. If you’re looking to make a public commitment to giving effectively, we recommend using their platform.

Both are tax-deductible for Dutch taxpayers.

Key questions to answer for yourself: How much will you give, as a percentage of income or a fixed amount? Where will you direct it: which cause areas, which organisations? And how will you decide: follow recommendations from Doneer Effectief or Giving What We Can, do your own research, or a mix?

A useful test for any donation: would this euro do more good than the same euro given to one of GiveWell’s top charities? That’s your personal bar. If you give to animal welfare or another cause, use the charities an evaluator in that area recommends instead. You don’t need a BOTEC to apply it. Often the honest answer is “I don’t know”, which is a good reason to give to a recommended charity.

Some people find it helpful to make a public commitment. Giving What We Can offers the 10% Pledge and a Trial Pledge, where you choose the percentage and the length, from six months to five years. Others prefer to keep their giving private. Either is fine. What matters is that you have a specific plan, not that you announce it. Starting at 1% and building from there is a perfectly good approach. The most important step is the first one.

Your political voice

Governments move far more money and affect far more lives than any charity. A small change in policy can matter more than a large change in giving. You won’t change policy on your own, but you have more influence than you might think, mostly by being specific and turning up where few others do.

Some ways to use it:

  • Vote, including in the elections people skip. Turnout in municipal, provincial and water board elections is much lower than in national ones, so each vote counts for more.

  • Join a party. Few people do. In many Dutch parties, members vote on the election programme and help shape the candidate list, which gives them more say than most people realise.

  • Respond to consultations. Many draft laws go out for public comment on internetconsultatie.nl before they’re finalised. Few people respond, so a specific, well-argued comment stands out.

  • Write to the right person. Each MP covers a set of topics as their party’s spokesperson (woordvoerder). A short, personal email to the right spokesperson about one issue is usually worth more than signing a petition. You can find members on the Tweede Kamer website.

  • Fund advocacy. Giving to organisations that lobby well can go further than your own time. The BOTEC you built in Week 3 is one way to think about whether it does.

A caution: politics is where it’s easiest to do harm with good intentions. Pick issues you’ve thought about carefully, be honest about your uncertainty, and keep to the same reasoning standards you’ve practised on this course. And it’s fine if this isn’t your pathway.

Read: Does your vote matter? What the research says, 80,000 Hours (5 mins).

Key questions to answer for yourself: Which issue that politics could move matters most to you? What’s one concrete action you’ll take this year?

Being a multiplier

If you help one other person give 10% of their income effectively, you’ve doubled the impact of your own giving. If you help someone find a career where they do much more good, you may have done more than you’ll manage directly in years. That’s the idea behind the multiplier pathway: some of the most valuable things you can do work through other people. It’s what we do at EA Netherlands.

It’s also easy to get wrong. Nobody likes being preached at, and pushing people tends to backfire. What works is usually quieter:

  • Talk about what you’re doing when people ask, honestly and without pressure.

  • Share something useful at the right moment: a good article, our free self-paced course, a career resource.

  • Help organise something: a giving game at work, a discussion evening, a fundraiser.

  • Help others in the community: run an event, mentor someone newer, or facilitate a future cohort of this course.

Apply the same thinking you’ve used all course. Would they have done it anyway? Is the good you’re adding worth the time it takes? Coefficient Giving uses a bar for work that raises money for effective charities: at least $2 raised for every $1 spent. It’s a useful test if you’re planning a fundraiser, a giving talk or a sponsored event. Will it raise at least twice what it costs, including the value of your time?

Read: Building effective altruism, 80,000 Hours (10 mins).

Getting involved with the Dutch and the international EA community

Whatever pathways you choose, stay connected. Plans made alone tend to drift. And you’re lucky enough to live in a country with one of the world’s largest EA communities.

  • WhatsApp community

  • Events in the Netherlands

  • International conferences

  • Co-working in Amsterdam
